steps.label: Combine the three cosines
steps.margin_note: No separate mark at this length. Pair two cosines, use the angle sum on the half angle, and write cos C in sines so both terms carry sin(C/2).
steps.memory_tip: Pair two cosines and write the third as 1 − 2sin²(C/2), so every term carries sin(C/2).

recall.must_convey: That cos A + cos B is combined to 2 sin(C/2) cos((A−B)/2) and cos C written as 1 − 2sin²(C/2).

get everything in terms of sin of C over two

steps.why: Two of the three cosines are combined into one product and the third is written in half angles, so the whole condition holds only two unknowns: sin(C/2) and cos((A−B)/2).
common_mistakes: Writing cos((A+B)/2) = cos(C/2) and losing the complement.
Using cos C = 2cos²(C/2) − 1, which does not match the sine that appears.

steps.label: Form a quadratic in sin(C/2)
steps.margin_note: One of the two marks. The unknown is sin(C/2); cos((A−B)/2) is the coefficient. A real root needs b² − 4ac ≥ 0.
steps.memory_tip: Treat sin(C/2) as the unknown. A real root needs b² − 4ac ≥ 0, which here is 16cos²((A−B)/2) − 16 ≥ 0.

recall.must_convey: That the equation is quadratic in sin(C/2) and a real root forces 16cos²((A−B)/2) − 16 ≥ 0.

steps.why: sin(C/2) is a real number, so the quadratic it satisfies must have a real root. That single requirement is what forces cos²((A−B)/2) to its largest possible value, 1.
common_mistakes: Treating cos((A−B)/2) as the unknown instead of sin(C/2).

steps.label: Read off the three angles
steps.margin_note: The other mark. cos²((A−B)/2) ≥ 1 and ≤ 1 force equality, and (A−B)/2 lies strictly between −90° and 90°, so the cosine is +1.
steps.memory_tip: A cosine is never more than 1, so ≥ 1 forces exactly 1, which means A = B. Then the quadratic becomes a perfect square.

lines.text: ∴ A = B = C = 60°, so it is equilateral

recall.must_convey: That cos²((A−B)/2) = 1 forces A = B, and the quadratic then becomes (2sin(C/2) − 1)² = 0, giving C = 60°.
accept: a cosine cannot be more than one so it must equal one and A equals B
put cos equal to one back and the quadratic is a perfect square
sin C over two is a half so C is sixty degrees and all three are sixty
cos value one kanna ekkuva undadu, so A equals B
the perfect square gives sin half C equals one half

steps.why: A cosine can never exceed 1, so the inequality can only hold as an equality. That fixes A = B, and putting cos((A−B)/2) = 1 back leaves a perfect square that fixes C.
common_mistakes: Stopping at A = B and calling the triangle isosceles.
Taking cos((A−B)/2) = −1, which no angle of a triangle allows.
